title: Nepal Buddhist Circuit: Sites, Route and Days Needed
meta_description: Nepal Buddhist circuit guide: Lumbini, Tilaurakot (Kapilavastu), Kudan, Niglihawa, Gotihawa, Ramagrama and Devdaha. Route, distances, days needed and costs.
summary: Nepal's Buddhist circuit covers seven sites within about 60 km of Lumbini: Lumbini itself, Tilaurakot (ancient Kapilavastu), Kudan, Gotihawa, Niglihawa, Ramagrama and Devdaha. Based in Lumbini, you can see them all in four to five nights by private car, or link them with Kushinagar and Sarnath in India via the Sonauli border.

sections.heading: What the Nepal Buddhist circuit covers
paras: The best-known Buddhist pilgrimage sites are spread across north India and southern Nepal. India holds Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment, Sarnath, where he gave his first sermon, and Kushinagar, where he died. Nepal holds the beginning of the story: his birth at Lumbini, his childhood and renunciation at Kapilavastu, and the homes of his mother's Koliya clan at Devdaha and Ramagrama.

All the Nepal sites lie in the western Terai, within Rupandehi, Kapilvastu and Nawalparasi West districts. They are flat, low-lying and linked by paved roads, so the circuit is physically easy. What it demands is time and a good guide, because outside Lumbini the remains are modest brick mounds and broken pillars whose meaning lies in the stories behind them.

sections.heading: The seven sites, one by one
paras: Lumbini is the anchor: the Maya Devi Temple with its marker stone, Ashoka's pillar of about 249 BCE, the sacred pond and the international monastic zone. Tilaurakot, 27 km west near Taulihawa, is the walled city identified with Kapilavastu, where Siddhartha lived until he left through the eastern gate at 29. The small Kapilvastu Museum displays pottery and coins from its excavations.

Kudan, south of Taulihawa, is linked with Nigrodharama, the grove where the Buddha met his father after enlightenment and ordained his son Rahula. Gotihawa, nearby, has the stump of an Ashoka pillar beside a stupa associated with Krakuchchanda Buddha. Niglihawa, north-east of Taulihawa, has a broken Ashoka pillar whose inscription records the enlargement of Kanakamuni Buddha's stupa and contains the earliest known written use of the word stupa.

To the east, Ramagrama near Parasi is the Koliya relic stupa, believed to be the only one of the eight original relic stupas never opened. Devdaha, near Butwal, was the Koliya capital and the home of Maya Devi and her sister Prajapati Gautami, who raised the Buddha and became the first nun.

sections.heading: How many days you need
paras: The circuit groups naturally into three outings from a Lumbini base. One day for Lumbini itself, with the Sacred Garden at dawn and the monastic zone in the afternoon. One day, or a long half-day, for the Kapilavastu cluster of Tilaurakot, Kudan, Gotihawa and Niglihawa, about 80 km of driving in total. One day for Ramagrama and Devdaha, about 150 km and 4.5–5 hours of driving.

That makes three full days on the ground, which means four nights with arrival and departure, or five nights if you want a slower pace, a meditation morning or a visit to the crane wetlands. With only two nights, focus on Lumbini and Tilaurakot. Pilgrims who want to sit, chant or meditate at each site should lean towards the longer plan.
list: 3 nights: add Kudan, Gotihawa and Niglihawa
4–5 nights: the full circuit including Ramagrama and Devdaha
7 nights or more: add Kushinagar and Sarnath in India via Sonauli

sections.heading: Joining the Indian Buddhist sites
paras: Many pilgrims combine Nepal with India in one journey. Kushinagar, where the Buddha passed away, is about 175 km from Lumbini via the Sonauli border and Gorakhpur, five to six hours by road. Sarnath, beside Varanasi, is about 330 km away, and Bodh Gaya roughly 250 km beyond Varanasi. Shravasti, where the Buddha spent many rainy seasons, is reached from the Nepalgunj side or by a longer drive via Balrampur.

The usual overland link is Varanasi or Bodh Gaya to Kushinagar, then across the border at Sonauli to Lumbini, ending in Gorakhpur or flying out from Bhairahawa. Indian citizens cross with a passport or voter ID. Foreign nationals need a Nepal visa, available on arrival at Belahiya, and an Indian visa valid for land entry if they return to India at Sonauli; an Indian e-Visa does not currently allow entry there. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Best season and daily rhythm
paras: October to March is the pilgrim season, with dry days of 18–28 °C. February, March, October and November are ideal. December and January bring cold, foggy mornings that can delay flights and make early drives slow. April to June is very hot, often 38–42 °C, though Buddha Jayanti, on the full moon of Baisakh in April or May, draws thousands to Lumbini despite the heat. The June to September monsoon brings humidity, mosquitoes and muddy site paths.

Whatever the season, plan each day around the sun. Leave at 7–7.30 am for outlying sites, return to Lumbini for lunch and rest in the heat, and spend late afternoons in the monastic zone or at evening chanting.

sections.heading: Costs and booking tips
paras: For Indian nationals, a 5-night Nepal Buddhist circuit with 3-star hotels, breakfast and dinner, private car, guide and entry fees starts at about ₹34,000 per person on a twin-sharing basis; the foreign-national rate is about US$ 430, reflecting higher entry fees. Groups of eight or more save by travelling in a minibus. Flights from Kathmandu to Bhairahawa are extra.

Book hotels early for Buddha Jayanti and for October and November, when monastery groups from Sri Lanka, Thailand and Myanmar travel. A guide who knows the sites matters more here than almost anywhere else in Nepal: signage at Kudan, Gotihawa and Devdaha is limited, and the experience depends on the stories told well.

faqs.q: What are the Buddhist sites in Nepal?
faqs.a: The main Buddhist sites in Nepal's Terai are Lumbini (birthplace), Tilaurakot (ancient Kapilavastu), Kudan, Gotihawa, Niglihawa, Ramagrama and Devdaha. In the Kathmandu Valley, Swayambhunath and Boudhanath are major stupas, and Namo Buddha near Dhulikhel is another pilgrimage site. This guide covers the Terai circuit around Lumbini.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for the Nepal Buddhist circuit?
faqs.a: Four to five nights based in Lumbini covers all seven Terai sites comfortably: one day for Lumbini, one for the Kapilavastu cluster and one for Ramagrama and Devdaha, plus arrival and departure. With two nights, focus on Lumbini and Tilaurakot.

faqs.q: Is Kapilavastu in Nepal or India?
faqs.a: Both countries claim it. Nepal identifies Kapilavastu with Tilaurakot near Taulihawa, a walled city with gates and a moat dated to the Buddha's era. India points to Piprahwa in Uttar Pradesh, where a relic casket inscription was found. The question is unresolved, and many pilgrims visit both.

faqs.q: Which is better: Nepal or India Buddhist circuit?
faqs.a: They complement each other. Nepal holds the birth and early life sites, India the enlightenment, first sermon and passing. If you can, combine them overland through Sonauli: Bodh Gaya or Sarnath, Kushinagar, then Lumbini and Kapilavastu, over 8–12 days.

faqs.q: What is the cost of a Nepal Buddhist circuit tour?
faqs.a: Our 5-night circuit starts at about ₹34,000 per person for Indian nationals or US$ 430 for foreign nationals, twin sharing, with 3-star hotels, breakfast and dinner, private car, guide and entry fees. Groups pay less per person. Flights to Bhairahawa are extra.

faqs.q: Can elderly pilgrims do the Buddhist circuit?
faqs.a: Yes. Every site is on flat ground, cars can park close to entrances and walks are short. The longest day involves about five hours of driving with breaks. Battery rickshaws can replace bicycles in Lumbini, and wheelchairs can be arranged with notice.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for the Buddhist sites?
faqs.a: It is strongly recommended. Outside Lumbini, signs are few and the remains are modest. A guide explains the history, archaeology and texts behind each site, finds the right village roads and handles tickets. Our circuit packages include a dedicated guide.

faqs.q: Can monks and nuns get special arrangements?
faqs.a: Yes. We arrange early starts for chanting, vegetarian meals, meals before noon for those who observe that rule, and extra time for puja at each site. Larger temple groups travel by minibus. Tell us your tradition and requirements when booking.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for the Buddhist circuit?
faqs.a: Stay in Lumbini, which is central to all the sites. Buddha Maya Gardens and Lumbini Hokke Hotel are comfortable 3-star options near the Sacred Garden. A final night in Bhairahawa, at Hotel Nirvana for example, suits early flights or border crossings.
